title: Chicago's food inspection forecasting model finds critical violations 7.5 days earlier in a double-blind retrodiction
summary: Double-blind retrodiction of 1,637 Chicago inspections (Sept-Oct 2014): the model would have found 69% of critical-violation sites in the first half of the work versus 55%, 7.5 days earlier.
account: Chicago's Department of Innovation and Technology and Department of Public Health, with pro bono data scientists from Allstate Insurance and the Civic Consulting Alliance, built a model that assigns each of the city's 15,000+ food establishments a likelihood of a critical violation from predictors such as previous critical or serious violations, three-day average high temperature, nearby garbage and sanitation complaints, facility type, nearby burglaries, licenses, time since last inspection, length of operation and the inspector assigned. In a double-blind retrodiction, the Department of Public Health inspected 1,637 establishments in its normal order during September and October 2014; 258 (almost 16%) had at least one critical violation, 141 (55%) found in the first month. Re-ordering the same inspections by the model's probabilities would have found 178 (69%) in the first half of the work, on average 7.5 days earlier, with an additional 37 establishments cited in the first month. The Harvard Ash Center's Data-Smart City Solutions wrote up the pilot on 19 May 2015, which is the date used here because the city page carries no date; the code is open source in R.
purpose: Forecast which Chicago food establishments are most likely to have critical sanitation violations so that inspectors visit them first.
system: Food Inspection Forecasting (predictive analytics model, open-sourced in R)
developer: City of Chicago Department of Innovation and Technology with the Department of Public Health, Allstate Insurance data scientists and the Civic Consulting Alliance
taxonomy_note: General benefit because the 7.5-day gain comes from a simulation applied to a fixed two-month inspection record, not from a live re-ordering of inspections; depths are null. The city page is an official report by the body that built and uses the tool; the Data-Smart article is an independent write-up. The fetched sources describe a probability model over a dozen variables but do not name the algorithm, so whether it is machine learning rather than conventional statistics is not stated.

ratings.reason: The sources document a retrospective simulation (69% vs 55% found in the first half; 7.5 days earlier) and no live-deployment outcome.
Earlier discovery 'potentially after patrons became ill' is stated as a rationale; no illness outcome is documented.

ai_role.statement: Developer and deployer are the same body: the City of Chicago built the model in-house with pro bono partners and the Department of Public Health is the user. The evaluation re-scored inspections after they were completed, so the model did not change any inspection in the pilot. Model type is not stated in the fetched sources.

evidence.citation: City of Chicago. Food Inspection Forecasting: Optimizing Inspections with Analytics. chicago.github.io (undated; copyright 2014-2017).
evidence.title: Food Inspection Forecasting - City of Chicago
evidence.quote: Over the two month pilot, establishments with violations were found, on average, 7 and a half days earlier.

evidence.citation: Thornton S. Delivering Faster Results with Food Inspection Forecasting: Chicago's Analytics-Driven Plan to Prevent Foodborne Illness. Data-Smart City Solutions, Harvard Ash Center, 19 May 2015.
evidence.title: Delivering Faster Results with Food Inspection Forecasting
evidence.quote: When using an analytics-based procedure, Chicago was able to discover critical violations, on average, seven days earlier than if they had used the traditional inspection procedure.

produced_by: Open inspection, 311 complaint, business license and weather data on the city's data portal
Fewer than three dozen inspectors for 15,000+ establishments, so ordering matters
A fixed two-month inspection record to re-score
must_hold: The predictor set (prior violations, nearby sanitation complaints, facility type, days since last inspection, inspector) remains available

headline: Chicago's model finds critical violations 7.5 days earlier
metric: 69% of critical-violation sites in the first half of the work versus 55%, 7.5 days earlier
